TOPICS: inspection findings, service ratings, safety and effectiveness concerns, staff practices, care quality, regulatory compliance, registered manager role, inspection methodology

TEXT_EVIDENCE:
- The inspection took place on 7 and 10 July 2015 and was unannounced (Page 1)
- This was the first inspection since the provider was registered with CQC (Page 1)
- The home is registered to provide accommodation for up to 32 people (Page 1)
- At the time of inspection, 28 people were living there, some with physical disabilities or dementia (Page 1)
- Care was not safe due to unsafe medicine management and unaddressed safeguarding incidents (Page 1)
- Risks to people's health were not always assessed or reduced (Page 2)
- Staff were not always respectful when addressing people or recording information (Page 2)
- The provider did not ensure appropriate processes were followed to protect people's rights when they lacked mental capacity (Page 2)
- Staff practice was not monitored effectively, and some staff were not up to date with necessary training (Page 2)
- People enjoyed the food, which was plentiful and presented appealingly, with choices of main meal and dessert (Page 2)
- Some people did not have access to meaningful activities, and a recommendation was made to the provider (Page 2)
- The environment was adapted for people with dementia, with accessible and well-maintained outside areas (Page 2)
- Staff responded to call bells in a timely manner and promoted independence (Page 2)
- Multiple breaches of the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014 were found (Page 2)
- The registered manager did not always report notifiable incidents to CQC or the local authority safeguarding team (Page 2)
- Some staff were unaware they were using unlawful restraint on people whose behavior placed themselves and others at risk (Page 2)
- The service was not safe due to poor medicine management, insufficient evening/night staff, unassessed risks, and mishandled safeguarding incidents (Page 3)
- The service was not effective due to outdated staff training, lack of monitoring, and use of unlawful restraint (Page 3)
- The service was not always caring as staff did not always address people respectfully or support their communication needs (Page 3)
- The service was not always responsive due to inaccurate care records, though complaints were handled timely and enjoyable activities were arranged (Page 3)
- The service was not always well-led due to notifiable incidents not being sent to CQC and ineffective quality assurance checks (Page 3)
- People enjoyed the food provided and the environment was adapted for safe outdoor access (Page 3)
- Staff promoted a friendly and jovial atmosphere in the home (Page 3)
- The registered manager was supportive to staff and available for advice and guidance (Page 4)
- The inspection was carried out under Section 60 of the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Page 5)
- We spoke with 20 of the 28 people living in the home and six relatives (Page 5)
- We observed staff providing care and support to people in the lounges and during the lunchtime meal in the dining room (Page 5)
- We looked at care plans and associated records for eight people living in the home (Page 5)
- We checked staff duty records, two recruitment files, records of complaints and accidents and incidents, medicine administration records, staff and residents' meeting minutes, quality assurance records and some of the provider's policies, procedures (Page 5)

SECTION: Detailed findings (Pages 5-15)

TOPICS: inspection methodology, safety, effectiveness, caring, responsiveness, well-led, regulatory breaches, staffing, medicines management, safeguarding, dignity, care planning, training, supervision, leadership, complaints procedure

TEXT_EVIDENCE:
- The inspection was carried out under Section 60 of the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Page 5)
- The inspection took place on July 7 and 10, 2015, and was unannounced (Page 5)
- The inspection team included two inspectors and an expert by experience in elderly care (Page 5)
- We spoke with 20 of the 28 people living in the home and six relatives (Page 5)
- We observed staff providing care and support to people in the lounges and during the lunchtime meal in the dining room (Page 5)
- We looked at care plans and associated records for eight people living in the home (Page 5)
- We checked staff duty records, two recruitment files, records of complaints and accidents and incidents, medicine administration records, staff and residents' meeting minutes, quality assurance records and some of the provider's policies, procedures (Page 5)
- Residents felt safe, with one saying staff "fuss over me like I was a puppy" (Page 6)
- Four injury records were not investigated or reported in line with policy (Page 6)
- Allegations of financial abuse were dismissed as "paranoia" or "UTI" (Page 6)
- The failure to respond to incidents breached regulation 13 (Page 6)
- Risks to health and safety were recorded but not always up to date (Page 6)
- A person's head injury monitoring was only recorded for one hour instead of 24 hours (Page 6)
- A fall risk assessment did not state what actions staff could take (Page 6)
- There were 28 people in the home, with 10-11 requiring two staff (Page 6)
- Staffing levels were insufficient in the evening, leading to inadequate monitoring (Page 6)
- Records showed two people became confused at night due to staffing shortages (Page 6)
- A breach of regulation 18 occurred due to insufficient staffing levels, which left one staff member to meet the needs of 27 people over three floors (Page 7)
- A breach of regulation 12 occurred due to the failure to manage medicines safely (Page 7)
- Medicines were stored in a warm room without temperature monitoring, compromising their effectiveness (Page 7)
- One person received PRN pain relief without being asked if they needed it, potentially leading to overmedication (Page 7)
- No pain assessments or pain care plans were in place for people unable to communicate pain (Page 7)
- One person's eye drops were prescribed twice daily but only provided once a day for five weeks (Page 7)
- Two people were prescribed creams that were not being used, and one cream could not be found (Page 7)
- One person was given a medicine not detailed on their MAR (Page 7)
- Records of competency checks were missing for two of four staff checked (Page 7)
- Medicines stocks were inaccurate for three medicines (two with excess, one with missing tablets) (Page 7)
- The home's medicines policy was based on NICE guidance but was not comprehensive enough (Page 7)
- The service was rated "Inadequate" at the top right (Page 8)
- Residents said, "I'm well looked-after" and "everything is lovely" (Page 8)
- Relatives said, "[my relative] gets absolutely brilliant care" (Page 8)
- Staff induction for a member starting in January 2015 consisted of a checklist and one supervision meeting (Page 8)
- The provider's policy required six supervisions per year, but only three were recorded (Page 8)
- Staff had received Mental Capacity Act training in 2011, which should have been repeated after three years (Page 8)
- Two staff described actions that amounted to restraint when a person resisted personal care (Page 8)
- The service had two contradictory policies on restraint (Page 8)
- The failure to ensure people were not unlawfully restrained was a breach of regulation 13 (Page 8)
- The failure to ensure appropriate staff induction, supervision, and training was a breach of regulation 18 (Page 8)
- Three people were indicated to lack capacity in care records (Page 8)
- Three people had bed rails due to fall risk; the decision was documented but not their capacity to consent (Page 9)
- Applications for Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards (DoLS) were made for three people, but there was no record of mental capacity assessment (Page 9)
- The failure to implement the MCA 2005 code of practice was a breach of regulation 11 of the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Page 9)
- People had access to district nurses, GPs, mental health professionals, chiropody, optician services, and hospital appointments (Page 9)
- The home provided nutritious food with choices, specialist diets (e.g., pureed, thickened fluids), and snacks at 9pm (Page 9)
- The building was adapted for dementia, with bright-colored handrails, chairs, and toilet doors, extra lighting, and a sensory garden (Page 9)
- Residents reported being treated with kindness and respect, with comments like "they're wonderful girls" and "I'm very happy" (Page 10)
- Staff used disrespectful terms in records ("feeds", "toileted", "commoded") and frequently referred to people as "love", "sweetheart", "mate", and "darling" instead of by name (Page 10)
- A staff member was observed calling out to another, "can you come and sort [person's name] out", which drew attention to a resident who had removed clothing, failing to protect their dignity (Page 10)
- One person was very hard of hearing; staff said they would write things down in large letters, but this practice did not happen during the inspection (Page 10)
- A staff member addressed a room of six people (four females, two males) by saying, "right then ladies, would you like to watch a film?", ignoring the two males and others' preferences (Page 10)
- A birthday celebration offered snacks and sherry to six people, but two others in an adjoining lounge were not invited or offered anything, despite the care plan stating one needed encouragement to join activities (Page 10)
- The failure to treat people with respect and dignity was a breach of regulation 10 of the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014 (Page 10)
- One staff member effectively communicated with a person with communication difficulties by speaking clearly and using gestures to guide them to the toilet (Page 10)
- Staff chatted with residents after lunch about holidays and knitting (Page 10)
- People's needs for end-of-life care were not recorded or reviewed (Page 10)
- The service had a 'just in case' box containing items to manage symptoms effectively (Page 11)
- There was no care plan in place for the person's end of life needs and wishes (Page 11)
- Staff were unaware of the person's end of life wishes, despite care being described as "wonderful" and "couldn't be better" (Page 11)
- Staff promoted independence by observing residents and only intervening when necessary, such as offering to cut food (Page 11)
- People were able to bathe using their en-suite facility and make choices like when to call a doctor or nurse (Page 11)
- A pleasant and jovial atmosphere was promoted during the lunchtime meal with background music and social interaction (Page 11)
- People could stay in their rooms if they preferred privacy and were observed going to their rooms at any point during the day (Page 11)
- One relative said aspects of care could be improved, specifically treating people as individuals (Page 12)
- A person had three falls between two care plan reviews, with no plan to prevent further falls (Page 12)
- A person's care records noted they could become frustrated and cross, but no triggers or care plans were recorded (Page 12)
- One person's activity record showed 11 activities in 19 weeks, seven of which were "nails cleaned" or "manicure" (Page 12)
- The failure to ensure care records reflected current needs was a breach of regulation 9 of the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulation Activities) Regulations 2014 (Page 12)
- People said they would complain if they wanted to and would speak to the registered manager (Page 12)
- The provider's complaints policy did not specify response times or provide contact details for escalation (Page 12)
- The service "Requires improvement" as stated in the top right corner (Page 13)
- The medicines audit was carried out monthly but was not thorough; the most recent was on 01 July 2015 (Page 13)
- The audit did not cover storage, temperature control, or disposal of medicines (Page 13)
- Staff practice was not monitored effectively; formal supervisions were infrequent (Page 13)
- Care plans were not updated to reflect changes in people's needs, with examples of a person no longer using a hoist and another needing pureed food (Page 13)
- A moving and handling risk assessment was out of date (Page 13)
- The registered manager failed to notify CQC of notifiable incidents, including suspected abuse and a grade four pressure injury (Page 13)
- The failure to maintain accurate records was a breach of regulation 17 (Page 13)
- The failure to notify CQC was a breach of regulation 18 (Page 13)
- People's feedback was sought and acted upon, with positive survey results (Page 13)
- Residents' meetings were held twice a year, with the most recent in January 2015 (Page 14)
- The most recent staff meeting was in May 2015 (Page 14)
- The registered manager and deputy manager were available to assist staff with guidance (Page 14)
- Staff could gain further qualifications if they wanted to, and one staff member said they were "really grateful for the opportunity" (Page 14)
- The service "Requires improvement" (indicated by a red dot) (Page 14)
- The provider did not ensure sufficient numbers of staff were available in the evening and at night; staff practice was not effectively monitored and training was not up to date (Regulation 18) (Page 15)
- The provider did not ensure the MCA 2005 code of practice was implemented to protect the rights of people who lacked mental capacity (Regulation 11) (Page 15)
- People were not always treated with dignity and respect (Regulation 10) (Page 15)
- People did not always receive appropriate care and treatment which met their needs and reflected their preferences (Regulation 9) (Page 15)
- No formal enforcement action was taken at this stage (Page 15)

- Residents felt safe, with one saying staff "fuss over me like I was a puppy" (Page 6)
- Four injury records were not investigated or reported in line with policy (Page 6)
- Allegations of financial abuse were dismissed as "paranoia" or "UTI" (Page 6)
- The failure to respond to incidents breached regulation 13 (Page 6)
- Risks to health and safety were recorded but not always up to date (Page 6)
- A person's head injury monitoring was only recorded for one hour instead of 24 hours (Page 6)
- A fall risk assessment did not state what actions staff could take (Page 6)
- There were 28 people in the home, with 10-11 requiring two staff (Page 6)
- Staffing levels were insufficient in the evening, leading to inadequate monitoring (Page 6)
- Records showed two people became confused at night due to staffing shortages (Page 6)
- A breach of regulation 18 occurred due to insufficient staffing levels, which left one staff member to meet the needs of 27 people over three floors (Page 7)
- A breach of regulation 12 occurred due to the failure to manage medicines safely (Page 7)
- Medicines were stored in a warm room without temperature monitoring, compromising their effectiveness (Page 7)
- One person received PRN pain relief without being asked if they needed it, potentially leading to overmedication (Page 7)
- No pain assessments or pain care plans were in place for people unable to communicate pain (Page 7)
- One person's eye drops were prescribed twice daily but only provided once a day for five weeks (Page 7)
- Two people were prescribed creams that were not being used, and one cream could not be found (Page 7)
- One person was given a medicine not detailed on their MAR (Page 7)
- Records of competency checks were missing for two of four staff checked (Page 7)
- Medicines stocks were inaccurate for three medicines (two with excess, one with missing tablets) (Page 7)
- The home's medicines policy was based on NICE guidance but was not comprehensive enough (Page 7)
- The service was rated "Inadequate" at the top right (Page 8)
- Residents said, "I'm well looked-after" and "everything is lovely" (Page 8)
- Relatives said, "[my relative] gets absolutely brilliant care" (Page 8)
- Staff induction for a member starting in January 2015 consisted of a checklist and one supervision meeting (Page 8)
- The provider's policy required six supervisions per year, but only three were recorded (Page 8)
- Staff had received Mental Capacity Act training in 2011, which should have been repeated after three years (Page 8)
- Two staff described actions that amounted to restraint when a person resisted personal care (Page 8)
- The service had two contradictory policies on restraint (Page 8)
- The failure to ensure people were not unlawfully restrained was a breach of regulation 13 (Page 8)
- The failure to ensure appropriate staff induction, supervision, and training was a breach of regulation 18 (Page 8)
- Three people were indicated to lack capacity in care records (Page 8)
- Three people had bed rails due to fall risk; the decision was documented but not their capacity to consent (Page 9)
- Applications for Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards (DoLS) were made for three people, but there was no record of mental capacity assessment (Page 9)
- The failure to implement the MCA 2005 code of practice was a breach of regulation 11 of the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Page 9)
- People had access to district nurses, GPs, mental health professionals, chiropody, optician services, and hospital appointments (Page 9)
- The home provided nutritious food with choices, specialist diets (e.g., pureed, thickened fluids), and snacks at 9pm (Page 9)
- The building was adapted for dementia, with bright-colored handrails, chairs, and toilet doors, extra lighting, and a sensory garden (Page 9)
- Residents reported being treated with kindness and respect, with comments like "they're wonderful girls" and "I'm very happy" (Page 10)
- Staff used disrespectful terms in records ("feeds", "toileted", "commoded") and frequently referred to people as "love", "sweetheart", "mate", and "darling" instead of by name (Page 10)
- A staff member was observed calling out to another, "can you come and sort [person's name] out", which drew attention to a resident who had removed clothing, failing to protect their dignity (Page 10)
- One person was very hard of hearing; staff said they would write things down in large letters, but this practice did not happen during the inspection (Page 10)
- A staff member addressed a room of six people (four females, two males) by saying, "right then ladies, would you like to watch a film?", ignoring the two males and others' preferences (Page 10)
- A birthday celebration offered snacks and sherry to six people, but two others in an adjoining lounge were not invited or offered anything, despite the care plan stating one needed encouragement to join activities (Page 10)
- The failure to treat people with respect and dignity was a breach of regulation 10 of the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014 (Page 10)
- One staff member effectively communicated with a person with communication difficulties by speaking clearly and using gestures to guide them to the toilet (Page 10)
- Staff chatted with residents after lunch about holidays and knitting (Page 10)
- People's needs for end-of-life care were not recorded or reviewed (Page 10)
- The service had a 'just in case' box containing items to manage symptoms effectively (Page 11)
- There was no care plan in place for the person's end of life needs and wishes (Page 11)
- Staff were unaware of the person's end of life wishes, despite care being described as "wonderful" and "couldn't be better" (Page 11)
- Staff promoted independence by observing residents and only intervening when necessary, such as offering to cut food (Page 11)
- People were able to bathe using their en-suite facility and make choices like when to call a doctor or nurse (Page 11)
- A pleasant and jovial atmosphere was promoted during the lunchtime meal with background music and social interaction (Page 11)
- People could stay in their rooms if they preferred privacy and were observed going to their rooms at any point during the day (Page 11)
- One relative said aspects of care could be improved, specifically treating people as individuals (Page 12)
- A person had three falls between two care plan reviews, with no plan to prevent further falls (Page 12)
- A person's care records noted they could become frustrated and cross, but no triggers or care plans were recorded (Page 12)
- One person's activity record showed 11 activities in 19 weeks, seven of which were "nails cleaned" or "manicure" (Page 12)

Key issues include inadequate induction processes, outdated training (e.g., Mental Capacity Act training from 2011), insufficient supervision, and contradictory policies on restraint use. pages.ocr_text: Is the service well-led? Our findings People said they were asked for their opinion of the service; this was both informally and formally with the use of surveys. One person said, "they come and ask me what I want and if I am happy". The registered manager said, "we try to get the views of residents as much as possible". A relative told us they had been sent a survey to complete. The registered manager said they monitored the quality of the service people received through audits. The medicines audit was carried out monthly and was not thorough. The most recent was recorded on 01 July 2015 and no actions were found to be necessary. The audit was limited in scope and involved checking that all medicines were in date. It did not cover the storage of medicines and staff said they thought the maintenance staff monitored the temperature of the medicines room. However, the maintenance staff said they did not do this and therefore no record was available to show medicines were kept at the appropriate temperature. The audit also did not cover the recording, handling or disposal of medicines. The registered manager said "I don't ask my staff to do anything I wouldn't do myself". Their vision for the home was to make it, "homely, with high standards of cleanliness, respect and dignity". They said they monitored this through training and support given to staff. However, the registered manager was not aware that staff did not always reflect their vision as they provided daily care to people. Staff practice was not monitored effectively. Formal supervisions and observation of staff practice was infrequent and did not enable the registered manager or provider to be informed of areas requiring improvement. Staffing levels during the evening and night had not been monitored in the light of people's increased needs for support. Reviews of the care people required were not thorough and care records were not audited to ensure the care people received was appropriate. The failure to effectively assess, monitor and improve the quality and safety of services was a breach of regulation 17 of the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014. The registered manager carried out an annual health and safety review of all areas of the home. This was supported by a weekly environmental audit where a selection of rooms and communal areas were looked at and actions were noted and completed. Staff used a maintenance record book to record repairs that were needed, and a maintenance member of staff was employed. People's care records were not always complete and up to date. The deputy manager said they reviewed each person's care plan monthly or more often if necessary. However we found that although the review was recorded, people's current needs were not reflected in their care plans. One care plan had not been updated following the person's admission to hospital a month previously. Their needs had changed, and for example, they were no longer able to use the hoist to be supported to transfer and were cared for entirely in bed now. Another person's care plan for eating showed they were able to eat independently however, the deputy manager said the person now had their food pureed and they needed assistance from staff to eat. Their care records did not show this change to their support needs. In a further example, the deputy manager confirmed a person's moving and handling risk assessment was out of date. The person required the use of a wheelchair to mobilise whereas their risk assessment showed they could weight bear. The failure to maintain an accurate and complete record of the care provided to each person was a breach of regulation 17 of the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014. Providers are required to inform CQC of notifiable incidents that occur in the home. The registered manager had not notified CQC, appropriately when notifiable events had taken place in the home. These included incidents of suspected abuse, and injuries sustained by people living in the home including the development of a grade four pressure injury. The failure to notify CQC of notifiable incidents was a breach of regulation 18 of the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Registration) Regulations 2009. People's feedback was sought and this was acted on. Results from the residents' and relatives' survey were positive, with most areas scored as "good" or "excellent". Two people had made comments which the registered manager had acted on. These were in relation to the meals offered and the time a person was offered a cup of tea. Several relatives had written to express their thanks for the care provided to their family member whilst at the home.
